Euronews reported that the pilot sites are due to be running by mid-2027, while the Guardian pointed to a start early next year, so the timetable is not consistent across sources.

Supporters argue that the hubs would shield the European asylum system and reduce the pull that draws irregular migrants to the continent. Danish immigration minister Morten Bødskov described the agreement as “a huge breakthrough”. German interior minister Alexander Dobrindt said such centres offer a constructive option for people whose home countries will not cooperate on returns.

Rwanda’s record is the main source of objections. A 2024 assessment by the US State Department concluded that security forces and civilian officials there could abuse human rights without being held to account, and it also raised concerns about free expression and forced labour. French Green MEP Mélissa Camara condemned the deal as “an agreement of shame”, warning that deportees would be sent thousands of kilometres from the EU with no firm guarantees for their rights.

Alain Berset, secretary general of the Council of Europe, said it was impossible to judge in advance what any return hub would involve, and that individual cases would have to be tested against the European convention on human rights. Picum, a pan-European group that campaigns for undocumented migrants, argued the scheme was doomed, saying that softer labels could not disguise the disruption of moving people to a country they have never known.
items.cav: The sources give different timelines for the pilot, and the figure of about 100 people reflects officials’ aims rather than a confirmed number. Details of Rwanda’s side of the arrangement and its legal basis are not spelled out, and the diplomatic sources cited by the Guardian are unnamed.
items.op: Moving people to a country they have never known, while they can still expect legal challenges, puts the rule of law under real strain. The five governments should publish the legal basis, safeguards and results of the trial, because those affected will have little power to contest what happens to them.

items.t: French football chief Philippe Diallo set to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency
items.s: UEFA has put French football federation chief Philippe Diallo forward as a late candidate for the FIFA presidency, setting up a contest with incumbent Gianni Infantino. The vote is scheduled for March 2027.
p: Philippe Diallo, who leads the French football federation, is poised to stand for the FIFA presidency as a late entrant in next year’s election. According to the report, European governing body UEFA proposed him on Monday after a meeting of its executive committee.

UEFA said Diallo had agreed to the invitation and that his candidacy still needs formal approval from the FFF Executive Committee, which is due to meet the following day. The body described him as having broad experience at every level of the sport.

Diallo is expected to face Japanese official Kozo Tashima and Infantino, who is seeking another term. Infantino, first elected in 2016, has come under heavy pressure since FIFA unveiled a contested private investment scheme in the summer. The plan would have let outside investors take stakes in a commercial subsidiary, and it was later dropped.

Critics across the game argued the governing body was trying to sell football off, while UEFA said national associations wanted renewed unity and trust. A FIFA spokesperson responded that Infantino would stand again and that nothing had changed since the president announced his plans in April.
Infantino has also been asked about his relationship with US President Donald Trump, though the report does not detail those questions.
The presidential election is due to take place at the 77th FIFA Congress on Thursday, 18 March 2027, in Rabat, Morocco.
items.cav: The UEFA statement and the FIFA spokesperson’s comments are reported by Euronews without independent confirmation, and the source does not detail the questions about Infantino’s ties to Donald Trump. Diallo’s candidacy is not final until the French federation ratifies it.
items.op: A federation leader entering a global election on a unity platform should face open scrutiny of his plans and of the investment scheme that damaged FIFA’s credibility. Voters in the football world deserve clear answers before March, not only assurances from the institutions involved.

items.t: Robert Pattinson confirmed as next James Bond as Denis Villeneuve directs Bond 26
items.s: According to the BBC, British actor Robert Pattinson has been confirmed as the next star of the James Bond series. The film, the 26th in the official run, has a director and writer in place, but no exact dates have been announced.
p: The series is about to be rebooted again, two decades after Daniel Craig made his debut as 007 in Casino Royale. The BBC describes the coming era as a new actor and a new creative team, arriving at a time when fans are waiting to see what shape it will take.

Pattinson is best known to many audiences for playing Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire and for his role in the Twilight films. The BBC notes that he has since appeared in The Batman and in Christopher Nolan’s recent adaptation of The Odyssey.

The broadcaster also points to his reputation within the industry for unusual choices, including independent, arthouse and experimental films. Its list of earlier credits includes The Lighthouse, Good Time, Tenet and The Lost City of Z.

Earlier reports had named other actors, among them Josh O’Connor, Jack Lowden and Callum Turner, as reportedly in contention. The BBC says several were thought to have reached final screen tests before Pattinson was chosen.
Production is expected to begin in 2027, with release pencilled in for 2028. The BBC stresses that film schedules can shift and that no exact dates have been announced.

Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival and Blade Runner 2049, is set to direct. He has said he grew up watching Bond films with his father and called the character “sacred territory”, adding that he intends to honour the tradition.

Steven Knight, the writer of Peaky Blinders and Burnt, will write the script. He told the BBC he planned to write the character, not the actor, and said he felt a responsibility to the source material.

The BBC’s explainer also recalls the series’ history, including Sean Connery’s return after George Lazenby’s single outing and Connery’s later appearance in the unofficial Never Say Never Again. Pierce Brosnan starred in four films, including The World Is Not Enough.
items.cav: The confirmation of Pattinson is presented by the BBC as established, but the release timeline is only expected, not fixed. The earlier summary naming O’Connor, Lowden and Turner as in the frame conflicts with the later report of a confirmed casting, and the sources do not explain how the decision was made.
items.op: A franchise this large shapes public culture, so the process behind major casting and creative choices matters. Audiences and fans deserve clear, timely information rather than rumours. Studios should be held to the same openness they expect from their marketing.

items.t: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang considered for comeback as US tightens remote access to advanced chips
items.s: Allies of Jensen Huang are reportedly campaigning for his return as Nvidia chief executive days after his resignation. Separately, the US Commerce Department has issued a rule limiting remote access to advanced computing chips.
p: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned last Thursday after revelations that he had at least two extramarital affairs, according to the Financial Times, which reported that Huang has discussed the possibility of returning with confidants. One of the affairs was with a woman accused of spying for China, and the other was with a subordinate.

Nvidia’s board has named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim chief executive. An open letter calling for Huang’s reinstatement has since drawn more than 165,000 signatories, including Elon Musk, Epic Games founder and chief executive Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator president Garry Tan and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick.

More than 7,500 of the signatories describe themselves as Nvidia employees. The live blog said that, if accurate, this would equal around 18% of the company’s workforce, but it did not confirm the figure. The investigation into Huang’s conduct has barely started, and Kress is due to present the company’s latest financial results shortly.

Separately, the US Commerce Department has issued an interim final rule to limit remote access to advanced chips by certain third countries. The government says the rule is meant to stop existing restrictions on sensitive American technology from being circumvented through data centres abroad.

Under the rule, licences will be required to reexport advanced chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. The move follows reports that Singapore-based Megaspeed, where suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang worked, transferred advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. The evidence does not independently confirm those reports, and Alice Huang is only a suspect.

Markets are also watching the planned stock market float of Anthropic, which is due to list on Thursday. The company had initially hoped for a $2tn valuation but may now list at a lower figure. Trading platform IG said its pre-IPO market had found a price around $1.4 trillion after recent volatility in tech, down from about $2 trillion at the end of October.
The live blog also reported that the FTSE 100 rose by as much as 29 points, or 0.25%, to 10,931 points, and described London’s index as resilient despite a sell-off in tech stocks.
items.cav: Much of the Huang story rests on a Financial Times report relayed secondhand, and the signatory and employee counts come from the open letter itself, which the live blog did not verify. The Anthropic figures also conflict: the source cites a $1.5bn valuation, which is far below the $1.4 trillion that IG cites, and the sources do not explain the gap.
items.op: Huang’s conduct is a matter for Nvidia’s board and its investigation, not for a petition of celebrity and industry signatures. Any return should wait for the findings to be made public. Transparency, not social-media momentum, should decide who leads one of the world’s most important chip companies.

items.t: Five EU countries expected to unveil deportation hub deal with Rwanda
items.s: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are reportedly set to announce a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, the first such facility outside the EU. Rights groups have already raised concerns about the choice of host.
p: Five EU countries are expected to announce a deal to create a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, according to diplomatic sources cited by the BBC and other outlets. Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands said in September that they were working towards an agreement with a non-EU country to host “return hubs” for people whose asylum claims have failed. Rwanda confirmed in August that it had begun “preliminary discussions” with several European states.

Details are expected at a press conference in Vienna on Monday, where a Rwandan delegation is also reported to be attending a migration conference. Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker told reporters he would “see next week in Vienna”, without giving details. According to diplomatic sources, the hub would start as a pilot hosting about 100 people, with each of the five countries possibly sending around 20 migrants. The countries hope the centre could be running in 2027.

The scheme would apply only to asylum seekers who have exhausted their legal options to remain in the EU, which distinguishes it from a British plan to send people to Rwanda for their claims to be processed. That UK deal never took off amid legal challenges and was scrapped by the Labour government in 2024. One source said Kigali is inclined to call the site a “welcome centre”, and that it would not be a detention facility.

The plan follows a recent EU reform that allowed the creation of hubs outside the bloc. Supporters argue such centres could speed up repatriations and deter irregular migration. Critics have likened them to “legal black holes” where migrants could be left in limbo with little oversight. The International Organization for Migration could play a supporting role, an IOM spokesperson said the agency was in discussions with some EU countries on such arrangements.

Human Rights Watch has voiced alarm over the choice of Rwanda, citing what it calls a well-established record of repression, arbitrary detention and support for armed rebels in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Its senior Africa researcher, Clementine de Montjoye, warned that paying Kigali to host deportations would finance a government accused of serious rights abuses. The EU Agency for Fundamental Rights has said any third country hosting a return hub must respect fundamental rights, including protection from sending people to places where they face serious risk of persecution.

The push comes as several EU governments face elections and pressure to show they can control migration. The European Border and Coast Guard Agency reported almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first ten months of the year, a 29% fall on the previous year, though October saw a 22% rise on September, driven largely by arrivals on the route to the Canary Islands. The EU says the plan complies with EU and international law, while human rights bodies say it could violate migrants’ rights.
items.cav: The details come from diplomatic sources and have not been confirmed by the governments involved before the planned announcement. Reports differ on whether the site would be a detention facility, with one source saying it would not be. Rwanda's government has not been quoted on the specific terms.
items.op: Deporting people to a country with a documented record of repression puts the rule of law at the centre of this deal. Governments should publish the legal safeguards, monitoring arrangements and the identity of anyone sent there before a single migrant boards a plane. Secrecy about a far-off hub will not restore public trust.

items.t: Xi, Trump and Putin to hold first trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Beijing says
items.s: Beijing says the leaders of China, the United States and Russia will discuss “world peace” at their first three-way summit this week. It has released few details about the agenda.
p: Beijing said on Monday that Presidents Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin will meet in the southern city of Shenzhen, with the meeting expected on Thursday alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. The Chinese foreign ministry, speaking through spokeswoman Mao Ning, described the talks as “in-depth exchanges” on safeguarding global peace and strategic stability among major powers. Beyond that language, officials offered little substance.

Mao Ning called the gathering one of “ground-breaking significance” during a briefing held hours after Beijing confirmed it. A French broadcaster’s report says the Kremlin and the White House had both already confirmed the three-way meeting. The DW report does not include that detail, so the point rests on a single outlet.

Trump has said nuclear disarmament and the Iran conflict will feature. Speaking at a Florida airport on November 8, he said the talks would cover denuclearization and that Washington was working to bring the Iran war to an end. He had earlier described the meeting as “interesting.” US officials, cited by AFP, said he is not expected to raise Russia’s war in Ukraine.

A Wall Street Journal report, which DW cites, claims Putin hoped the summit would produce a Ukraine peace deal favouring Moscow. That account is second-hand, and the governments involved have not confirmed it in the material provided.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who recently visited China, told the broadcaster ARD that Xi seemed irritated when asked whether Ukraine would be on the agenda. According to Steinmeier, Xi argued that the conflict is a European matter and that Europeans must have a seat at the table. On Friday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged Trump to avoid any surprises on Ukraine during the talks.

Arms control remains a sticking point. Washington wants China included in future nuclear agreements, whereas Beijing says the United States and Russia must first cut their large stockpiles. China had already turned down Trump’s proposal for wider disarmament talks after the US-Russia nuclear treaty lapsed in February. A State Department readout says Wang Yi and Marco Rubio agreed that “meaningful leader-level conversations” matter, and UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said a genuine denuclearization commitment would be a major achievement.

The Iran war, which started with US and Israeli strikes on February 28, has cooled somewhat, though key disputes are unsettled. Neither Washington nor Jerusalem is currently launching large attacks, while Tehran keeps pressing to control the Strait of Hormuz and continues to target vessels it regards as unauthorised. Pakistan-mediated US-Iran talks in April did not yield a lasting deal. China, a major economic partner of Tehran, has repeatedly offered to mediate and recently hosted Middle Eastern officials in an attempt to bring the parties back to negotiations.
items.cav: Beijing has given few details, so the agenda is known mainly from official phrases. The claim about Putin’s goals rests on a Wall Street Journal report cited second-hand, and Xi’s reaction comes only from Steinmeier’s account. The sources differ on whether the Kremlin and White House confirmed the meeting, and none says what, if anything, the leaders will agree.
items.op: Three leaders discussing nuclear weapons and Ukraine should not reach understandings out of public view. The public has a right to know what is promised and who would bear the cost. Vague talk of “world peace” is not accountability. Any outcome touching arms control or a neighbour’s war must be published and open to scrutiny.

items.t: Musk backs campaign to reinstate ousted Nvidia boss Jensen Huang as allies lobby for his return
items.s: Allies of Jensen Huang are pressing Nvidia’s board to bring back the former chief executive, who resigned last week amid reports of extramarital affairs. Elon Musk is among the backers of a petition, while the US Treasury Secretary has called for the company to look outside for its next leader.
p: Allies of Jensen Huang are trying to rally support for the former Nvidia chief executive to get his job back. He resigned last week after reports of two extramarital affairs, one of them with a woman suspected of spying for China, according to the BBC. SpaceX boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Epic Games, are among those backing a campaign urging the board to “Bring Jensen Back”.

An open letter on a website called “Stand with Jensen” asks the board to reinstate Huang while an independent investigation establishes the facts. The number of signatures reported varies by outlet. The BBC puts it above 175,000, the Guardian above 165,000 and Euronews above 160,000. The campaign says its supporters include current and former Nvidia employees, partners and shareholders. Euronews reports that more than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees.

The first affair, involving Alice Huang, had initially been expected to be weathered. Huang then resigned after a second relationship emerged, allegedly with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. The Financial Times reported that Huang has discussed a possible return with confidants. One ally told the paper that a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives was being assembled to lobby for him and to seek support from the White House.

Musk has argued that some of Nvidia’s key deals were agreements made on a handshake with Huang rather than written contracts, and that some of them could be lost without him. The claim is his own and has not been independently tested. Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, two large investors, have urged the board to keep “all options” open, including a possible return.

Not all voices are supportive. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Fox News that Nvidia needs “a dramatic shake-up” and should look outside the company for its next chief executive. The Guardian reports that he wants answers within 10 days on whether Nvidia knowingly allowed its most advanced chips to reach China and whether it had a culture of compliance with US export rules. The BBC reports that the case has also created tension between the Treasury and Commerce departments over shipments of high-end chips to Megaspeed, the Singapore company where Alice Huang was an executive until 2025. Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful business”.

The BBC understands that Huang’s reinstatement is unlikely while Nvidia’s internal investigations continue. Analyst Dan Ives called the idea “ridiculous” and said the best path was an external chief executive or Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who is currently leading the firm. Huang has agreed to testify before congressional committees, although the dates have not been confirmed. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday.
items.cav: The petition figures differ between outlets and cannot be checked independently. Details of the affairs, the alleged spying and the FBI investigation come from reports and from Trump’s own comments, not from Nvidia or official findings. Musk’s account of the deals is unverified, and Euronews’ claim about a 25% revenue share on H200 sales is not confirmed by the other sources.
items.op: Nvidia’s board owes shareholders and lawmakers a transparent account of what it knew about chip sales to China and why its chief left. Any reinstatement should follow published findings, not a petition with a large signature count. The real test is process, not popularity.

items.t: Helen Haines leaves hospital after both legs were amputated following alleged car attack
items.s: Independent MP Helen Haines has been discharged from a Melbourne hospital after an alleged October attack that cost her both legs. A man has been charged, and she is starting rehabilitation.
p: Haines, who sits as an independent, said she was “full of gratitude” after leaving the Alfred Hospital on Monday, according to a statement she released.

The 65-year-old was hit by a Toyota Land Cruiser on 19 October while standing beside her car in Wangaratta, a regional town in Victoria. The injuries she suffered later required both legs to be amputated.

Hospital staff said she had been discharged about four weeks after being flown in for emergency care. Haines said she has now begun the rehabilitation phase, which will take place in Melbourne for the foreseeable future.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he has been in regular contact with Haines and her relatives, and that the government is backing her, her family, her local community and her staff during her rehabilitation.

Police have laid charges against 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, including dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and a federal offence of harming a public official. He is presumed innocent unless a court finds otherwise.
Before entering parliament in 2019, Haines worked as a nurse and midwife. She has campaigned against corruption and for tougher climate policy.
The case has triggered wider discussion in Australia, where political violence is uncommon even though police have recorded a consistent increase in threats aimed at elected representatives.
items.cav: The attack is described as alleged, and the charges have not been tested in court. The evidence does not say what motive, if any, police have assigned, and it does not detail the state of the investigation.
items.op: Threats against elected officials are a rule-of-law issue, not a footnote. Whoever is responsible must face a fair trial, and authorities should publish what they are doing to protect members of parliament, so that public service does not depend on personal courage.

items.t: Estonia to close Russian border crossings after alleged GRU sabotage bid on drone maker
items.s: Tallinn says all its crossings with Russia will shut from 1 December, following what it describes as a foiled arson plot by Russia’s GRU military intelligence. Moscow has said it will check whether the plan is real.
p: Authorities in Estonia have stopped a plot that officials say targeted a drone factory with arson. The government links the scheme to Russia’s GRU military intelligence and has responded by announcing a shutdown of the frontier.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal posted on X that the GRU had commissioned a “sabotage attempt” against Threod Systems, a defence firm in Estonia, late on Saturday. In his account, heightened security and a rapid response by law enforcement prevented major harm. Chief prosecutor Astrid Asi later told reporters that eight people living in Latvia had been arrested.

Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on X that every Estonian-Russian crossing would close from 1 December, pointing to “clear evidence” of GRU involvement. He added that he had briefed his counterparts in Finland, Latvia and Lithuania. He warned that Moscow would face consequences for hostile acts, and said efforts to intimidate or destabilise Estonia would not go unanswered.

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova, speaking to the TASS news agency, said Moscow would first establish whether Tallinn truly intended to seal all crossings. She said that, if it did, Russia would regard the step as yet another instance of hostility toward Russia.

Michal framed the affair as one front in what he called a wider hybrid campaign against Europe, meant to weaken backing for Ukraine and increase pressure on Russia. Tallinn also recalls that in August the Tallinn-based subcontractor Milrem Robotics was the target of a similar arson attempt, and that Latvian nationals were detained in that case.

Estonia has three crossing points with Russia: Narva in the north, and Luhamaa and Koidula in the south. Russia halted vehicle traffic at Narva in February 2024, but pedestrians can still pass. These crossings remain among the few land links between Russia and the European Union that are still functioning.
items.cav: The GRU’s role rests on Estonian government statements, and the sources do not show the underlying evidence. The eight arrested people are suspects, and no charges or court findings are reported. Russia has only said it will verify the closure plan.
items.op: Sealing a border punishes ordinary travellers, families and businesses, and it should not become a reflex. If Tallinn believes the GRU ordered sabotage, it owes the public and the courts the evidence, and the suspects a fair process.

items.t: Australian MP Helen Haines leaves hospital four weeks after alleged car attack
items.s: Independent MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital and says she is now in the rehabilitation phase of her recovery. A man has been charged over the alleged attack, which police are still investigating.
p: Helen Haines, the independent MP for Indi, has left hospital roughly four weeks after she was allegedly struck by a car, according to the BBC. The incident took place on October 19 outside her office in Wangaratta, a town north-east of Melbourne, and it shocked the country.

In her first public remarks since the attack, Haines, 65, described her discharge as a positive step and thanked the staff at the Alfred hospital for their care. She said she was moving into the next stage of healing and was grateful for the large number of messages and the donations made to Save the Children in her name.
The BBC reports that Haines lost both of her legs. Her account of her condition is based on the broadcaster’s summary and has not been independently detailed in the material available.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with offences including dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and a federal offence of harming a public official. He has not yet entered a plea, and he is presumed innocent unless and until a court finds otherwise.

Victoria Police, assisted by the Australian Federal Police, says its investigation is continuing and that no motive has been established. Nugent’s father has said that he and his wife were longtime friends of Haines, while Nugent’s lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns.
Haines has campaigned for stronger climate action and helped set up a national anti-corruption commission. She entered parliament in 2019 after a career as a nurse and midwife.

Politicians, police and experts have argued that the tone of public debate is raising the risk of political violence, although the attack’s motive remains unclear. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he has been in regular contact with Haines and her family, and that support will continue during her rehabilitation.
items.cav: The sources do not establish a motive, and the link between heated public debate and the attack is a view put forward by politicians and experts rather than a finding. The loss of both legs is reported by the BBC summary, and the timing is described in different terms across the material.
items.op: Political violence cannot be read off a single case, but this one should sharpen attention on how public anger turns into personal threat. A clear, public account of the motive and a fair court process for Nugent matter as much as Haines’s recovery. Australia owes both to its public.

items.t: Singapore firm Megaspeed says suspected spy tied to Nvidia affair left its top role in 2025
items.s: Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that the reporting describes as Southeast Asia’s largest purchaser of Nvidia chips, says Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy linked to Nvidia’s former chief executive, left her executive post last year. The claim comes amid wider questions about whether high-end chips reached China despite US restrictions.
p: On Sunday, Megaspeed said it had opened an internal inquiry into its operations. The firm objected to reports that make claims about its business, supply chain and global activities without what it called “verifiable evidence”. It insisted that it operates lawfully and has brought in outside lawyers to lead the review.

Alice Huang, who is unrelated to Jensen Huang, was examined by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of a wider inquiry into Megaspeed and other firms. She is a suspect rather than a convicted person, and the reporting does not describe any verdict against her. Her departure date is disputed: Megaspeed says she left in August last year, while a Washington-based security analysis group, C4ADS, says she stepped down as a director near the end of 2023.

Jensen Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive after reports that he had allegedly been involved with Alice Huang and with another employee. The scandal has raised doubts about whether powerful chips sold in Southeast Asia could have been routed to China in breach of US export limits.

Congressman John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said on Sunday that Jensen Huang had agreed to give evidence to his panel and to the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees. Those committees had warned they would compel him through subpoenas if he refused. The session is expected to be closed to the public, and its dates have yet to be confirmed.
Moolenaar said the hearing should clarify how much sensitive material may have been reached, and whether the suspected spy shaped Nvidia’s outlook and the policies on advanced-chip exports.

The Financial Times reported that Jensen Huang was weighing a return to the company he helped found, a claim his representative declined to address. The BBC understands that a reinstatement looks highly unlikely while internal investigations at Nvidia remain open. For now, chief financial officer Colette Kress is running the company and is scheduled to report results on Tuesday, 17 November.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has urged Nvidia to pick its next chief executive from outside the firm. On Friday he faulted the Commerce Department, headed by Howard Lutnick, for weak oversight of high-end chip exports. He told CNBC that several agencies had pushed for months to add Megaspeed to the entity list, which restricts trade with listed foreign firms, but that Commerce controlled the decision. Lutnick is due to be questioned by the Senate Banking Committee next month.

Megaspeed is suspected of providing backdoor access to Nvidia chips for Chinese companies through data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. Singapore does not ban moving such chips to overseas firms, yet doing so can still violate US export rules, and Singapore says it expects companies under its authority to follow those rules. Megaspeed says its compliance frameworks cover US export requirements and local laws wherever it operates.
items.cav: The sources disagree on when Alice Huang left Megaspeed: one report points to August last year, while C4ADS says she stepped down near the end of 2023 yet remained “practically in control”. The allegations about Jensen Huang and the chip-diversion suspicions are unproven, and Megaspeed’s account is its own.
items.op: Export controls are only as credible as the agencies enforcing them, and secrecy over who held back a listing decision undermines public trust. Congress should press Commerce and Megaspeed for records in public wherever possible. Rule of law requires answers, not closed-door assurances.
